hints: Look at the curvature of P and Q with $I$ on the vertical axis: P flattens so gradient $I/V$ falls, while Q steepens so gradient $I/V$ rises.
Recall that gradient of an $I$-$V$ graph equals $1/R$, and that a filament heats up so its resistance increases with $V$ and $I$.
Compare R and S near $V = 0$: R has $I = 0$ until a threshold $V$ then a very steep rise, while S already has $I > 0$ at $V = 0$.
walkthrough: Identify the axes: $I$ is plotted against $V$, so the gradient at any point is $I/V = 1/R$ where $R$ is the resistance.
For a filament lamp, increasing $V$ increases $I$ and heating power, so temperature rises and metal filament resistance $R$ increases.
Increasing $R$ means $1/R$ decreases, so the $I$-$V$ curve must flatten with increasing $V$. That matches graph P, not graph Q which gets steeper.
For a semiconductor diode, reverse or small forward $V$ gives almost zero $I$, then above a threshold forward $V$ the current rises very sharply in one direction only.
Graph R shows $I = 0$ along the $V$-axis up to a threshold then a steep straight rise, while graph S wrongly shows $I > 0$ when $V = 0$. So the diode is R.
Lamp P with diode R matches the first row. This is option A.

A.explanation: P shows $I$ rising with decreasing gradient as heating raises resistance, and R shows zero $I$ until a threshold $V$ then a sharp rise for forward conduction.

B.explanation: P is correct for the lamp, but S is wrong for a diode because it shows significant $I$ at $V = 0$, whereas a diode has $I = 0$ below its threshold voltage.

C.explanation: Q shows $I$ rising with increasing gradient so resistance falling, which is opposite to a filament lamp heating up; R is correct for the diode.

D.explanation: Q has the wrong curvature for a lamp and S has non-zero $I$ at $V = 0$ with only a slow rise, which does not show diode threshold behaviour.
